name: Tool Authentication and Scoped Permissions
question: Whose credentials does each tool call carry, and for what?
summary: Each tool call the agent makes reaches a real API with some credential. Instead of one shared service key that can touch every customer, the user signs in and consents through OAuth 2.1 with PKCE, and the agent receives a delegated token for that user only. Each tool gets the narrowest scope it needs, access tokens live minutes and are renewed silently, and tokens sit in a vault that the tool layer reads, never in the prompt. Disconnecting revokes them, and every call is logged under the user. The MCP technique covers what a server must check; action policies decide whether a call is allowed; this is about the credentials the call carries.
useCases: Agents that act on a customer’s own accounts: portfolios, bank data, email, calendars
Connecting to remote MCP servers or SaaS APIs on behalf of many users
Anywhere an auditor asks which user a tool call acted for

items.detail: issued to the agent for one user after that user consents; calls act as that user
authorization code flow with an S256 code challenge, so a stolen code cannot be redeemed
one per tool and verb, such as portfolio:read or redeem:write; writes asked for when needed
access tokens last minutes to an hour; rotating refresh tokens renew them silently
encrypted, per user, outside the prompt; the tool layer attaches the token to the call
disconnecting revokes the refresh token; each call is logged with user, tool and scope

steps: List each tool with the API it calls and the narrowest scope it needs
Get a per-user token with OAuth 2.1 + PKCE, asking for read scopes first and writes only when needed
Keep tokens in a vault; the tool layer attaches them, the model only sees results
Use short-lived access tokens with rotating refresh, revoke on disconnect, and log every call under the user
pitfalls: One shared service key lets any prompt injection reach every customer’s account
A token pasted into the prompt can be echoed out by the model or land in traces and logs
Asking for every scope at sign-up means a read-only question carries redeem rights
remember: Act as the user, only for this tool, only for a few minutes. Keep the key out of the prompt.
caption: Illustrative: Dhan Disha, a fictional wealth app, with 50,000 users who connected their accounts to its assistant.

resource=MCP_URL)                             #@1  token is for this server
code = wait_for_redirect(user_id, url)        # the user signs in and consents
tok = refresh(tok.refresh_token)          # silent; rotates the refresh token
raise StepUpConsent(user_id, need)        # ask the user; never widen silently
return downscope(tok, need)                   # a token for this one tool
token = token_for(user_id, tool)              # the model never sees this
return result                                 # only data goes back to the model

steps.title: Sign in with OAuth 2.1 and PKCE
steps.text: connect() sends the user to the authorization server with a PKCE challenge: the SHA-256 of a random verifier. Only the holder of the verifier can swap the returned code for a token, so a code stolen from the redirect is useless. The resource parameter names the MCP server, so the token is valid there and nowhere else.

steps.title: One scope per tool
steps.text: Each of Dhan Disha’s five tools maps to one scope. Reading a portfolio needs portfolio:read; redeeming units needs redeem:write. downscope() hands each call a token carrying only its tool’s scope, so a read call cannot redeem.

steps.title: Consent to reads now, writes when needed
steps.text: At sign-up the user grants only the two read scopes. The first time the agent needs to redeem or change a mandate, token_for() raises StepUpConsent and the user sees exactly what is being added. The token is never widened silently.

steps.title: Short-lived tokens, silent refresh
steps.text: Access tokens last 15 minutes. When one is about to expire, the refresh token gets a new one without asking the user, and the refresh token itself is rotated. A leaked access token works for minutes, not days, and the user sees no extra prompts.

steps.title: Keep secrets in the vault, not the prompt
steps.text: Tokens live in an encrypted vault keyed by user. call_tool() fetches the token and attaches it to the HTTP call; the model only receives the tool’s result. A prompt injection can steer a call, but it cannot make the model reveal a secret it never saw.

steps.title: Log every call, revoke on disconnect
steps.text: Each call is logged with the user, tool and scope, so an auditor can see who each action was for. When a user disconnects, the refresh token is revoked at the authorization server and deleted from the vault, and access ends within 15 minutes.

Prompt injection cannot reach other customers or copy a secret it never saw
Every call is attributable to a named user who consented

Downstream APIs must support per-user tokens and fine-grained scopes

playgroundGuide.scenario: Dhan Disha, a fictional wealth app, has 50,000 users connected to its assistant, which uses five tools: get_portfolio, get_statements, start_sip, redeem_units and update_mandate. You decide whose credential each call carries, how narrow its scopes are, how long access tokens last and where secrets are kept, then see what a leak or a prompt injection could reach.
controls: Choose one shared API key for everyone, or a per-user OAuth token that each user consents to.
Choose broad scopes (every call carries all five) or one scope per tool, with write scopes added by step-up consent.
Pick the access-token lifetime and whether secrets sit in the system prompt or in a vault, or load a scenario.

outputs.name: Accounts exposed if a credential leaks
outputs.meaning: How many users’ accounts one leaked key or token opens, for how long, and with which rights.

outputs.name: Exposure (accounts × hours)
outputs.meaning: Accounts exposed multiplied by the hours the leaked credential keeps working.

outputs.name: Accounts a prompt injection can reach
outputs.meaning: How many accounts an injected instruction can steer the agent to act on, and whether it can copy the credential out.

outputs.meaning: Sign-in and consent screens a user sees, with the silent refreshes behind them.

presets.name: Shared key in the prompt
presets.expect: 50,000 accounts exposed for 2,160 hours (108,000,000 account-hours) with redeem rights; an injection reaches all 50,000 and can copy the key; 0 prompts; 0% attributable.

presets.name: Per-user token, broad, 24 h, vault
presets.expect: 1 account for 24 hours (24 account-hours), still with redeem rights; injection reaches 1 account and cannot copy the token; 0.03 prompts a day; 100% attributable.

presets.name: Per-user, per-tool, 1 h, vault
presets.expect: 1 account for 1 hour, read-only (1 account-hour); 0.23 prompts a day (about one every 4 days); 3 silent refreshes each, 150,000 in all; 100% attributable.

presets.name: Per-user, per-tool, 15 min, token in the prompt
presets.expect: 1 account for 15 minutes, read-only (0.25 account-hours), but an injection can make the model echo the token; 0.23 prompts and 6 silent refreshes a day (300,000 in all).

missions.text: Make a leaked credential expose one account, read-only, for an hour or less.
missions.hint: Per-user OAuth tokens, one scope per tool, and a 1-hour or 15-minute lifetime.

missions.text: Make a prompt injection reach only the current user, unable to copy the credential or redeem units.
missions.hint: Per-user tokens, per-tool scopes, and secrets in a vault instead of the prompt.

missions.text: Use 15-minute tokens while users see no more than one re-auth prompt every 4 days and every call is attributable.

tools.best: OAuthClientProvider runs discovery, PKCE, token exchange and refresh for MCP clients; you supply the token storage.
pros: Plug in your own vault through TokenStorage
cons: Client side only: scopes and consent live on the authorization server
tools.ex: A per-user VaultTokenStorage so each investor’s tokens are stored and refreshed separately.

tools.best: Stores users’ tokens for third-party APIs and hands the agent a fresh one per tool call.
pros: Refresh and storage handled for you
cons: A vendor in your token path
tools.ex: An assistant that reads a user’s Google Calendar with a token fetched per call, never stored by the agent.

tools.best: Your own authorization server: clients, scopes, consent screens, token exchange and revocation.
cons: A critical service to run and patch
tools.ex: Dhan Disha issuing 15-minute tokens with portfolio:read and redeem:write scopes.

tools.best: Encrypted secret storage with per-path policies, leases and an audit log.
pros: Keeps tokens out of code, prompts and traces
cons: Does not run OAuth flows for you

tools.best: An agent tool platform that runs per-user OAuth for each tool and asks the user when a new scope is needed.
pros: Per-user auth built into tool calls
cons: Tools run through a third party
tools.ex: An email assistant that asks the user to approve the send scope the first time it drafts a reply.

practice.scenario: Dhan Disha, a fictional wealth app, lets 50,000 investors connect their accounts to its assistant, which reaches the app’s MCP server through five tools: portfolio, statements, SIPs, redemptions and bank mandates. It used to call everything with one shared API key pasted into the system prompt. Now each investor signs in once with OAuth 2.1 and PKCE, consents to read scopes, and approves write scopes only when the assistant first needs them. Tokens last 15 minutes, refresh silently, live in a vault keyed by user, and every call is logged under the investor’s id.

industries.use: An assistant that reads holdings and places SIPs or redemptions only with the investor’s own consented token
Consent-based access to bank statements, where each consent names the data, the purpose and the expiry
An assistant reading one employee’s email and calendar with read scopes, asking again before it sends mail

practice.analogy: A hotel key card. Reception checks who you are and programs a card for your room only, valid until checkout. Lose it and one room is at risk for a day, and the front desk can cancel it. A master key taped to the lift would open every room, and nobody could tell whose door was opened by whom.

library.name: MCP Python SDK (mcp)
library.what: OAuthClientProvider plugs into the HTTP client: it discovers the authorization server from the MCP server’s protected resource metadata, runs the authorization code flow with PKCE, and refreshes tokens. You supply a TokenStorage, here backed by a per-user vault.

practice.note: vault, send_consent_link and wait_for_code stand for your secret store and web app. Class and function names follow the MCP Python SDK at the time of writing (streamablehttp_client may be named streamable_http_client in newer releases, and stateless protocol revisions may not need initialize()); check the SDK version you install.

samples.code:
from pydantic import AnyUrl
from mcp import ClientSession
from mcp.client.auth import OAuthClientProvider, TokenStorage
from mcp.client.streamable_http import streamablehttp_client
from mcp.shared.auth import OAuthClientInformationFull, OAuthClientMetadata, OAuthToken

MCP_URL = "https://mcp.dhandisha.example/mcp"


class VaultTokenStorage(TokenStorage):
    """One entry per user in the secret store. The model never sees these values."""

    def __init__(self, user_id: str):
        self.path = f"dhan-disha/{user_id}/mcp"

    async def get_tokens(self) -> OAuthToken | None:
        raw = await vault.read(self.path + "/tokens")
        return OAuthToken.model_validate_json(raw) if raw else None

    async def set_tokens(self, tokens: OAuthToken) -> None:
        await vault.write(self.path + "/tokens", tokens.model_dump_json())

    async def get_client_info(self) -> OAuthClientInformationFull | None:
        raw = await vault.read(self.path + "/client")
        return OAuthClientInformationFull.model_validate_json(raw) if raw else None

    async def set_client_info(self, info: OAuthClientInformationFull) -> None:
        await vault.write(self.path + "/client", info.model_dump_json())


def auth_for(user_id: str) -> OAuthClientProvider:
    async def on_redirect(url: str) -> None:        # show this user the consent screen
        await send_consent_link(user_id, url)

    async def on_callback() -> tuple[str, str | None]:
        return await wait_for_code(user_id)        # (code, state) from your redirect URI

    return OAuthClientProvider(
        server_url=MCP_URL,
        client_metadata=OAuthClientMetadata(
            client_name="Dhan Disha assistant",
            redirect_uris=[AnyUrl("https://app.dhandisha.example/oauth/callback")],
            grant_types=["authorization_code", "refresh_token"],
            response_types=["code"],
            scope="portfolio:read statements:read",  # write scopes are requested later
        ),
        storage=VaultTokenStorage(user_id),
        redirect_handler=on_redirect,
        callback_handler=on_callback,
    )


async def get_portfolio(user_id: str):
    async with streamablehttp_client(MCP_URL, auth=auth_for(user_id)) as (read, write, _):
        async with ClientSession(read, write) as session:
            await session.initialize()
            result = await session.call_tool("get_portfolio", {})
    audit_log(user=user_id, tool="get_portfolio", scope="portfolio:read")
    return result.content                        # only data goes back to the model

numericDrill.question: Dhan Disha’s assistant uses one shared API key for its 50,000 users, rotated every 90 days (2,160 hours). If the key leaks right after rotation, how many account-hours are exposed? (A per-user 15-minute token would expose 0.25.)
numericDrill.answer: 50,000 accounts × 2,160 hours = 108,000,000 account-hours. A per-user token with a 15-minute lifetime exposes 1 × 0.25 = 0.25 account-hours, 432 million times less.

interview.question: How should an agent’s tools authenticate to APIs on behalf of users?
interview.answer: With delegated per-user tokens, not a shared service key. The user signs in through OAuth 2.1 with PKCE and consents to named scopes; the token is bound to the target server with a resource indicator. Each tool gets the narrowest scope, writes are added by step-up consent, access tokens are short-lived with rotating refresh, and tokens live in a vault the tool layer reads. Revoke on disconnect and log every call under the user.

interview.question: Why must credentials never appear in the prompt?
interview.answer: Anything in the context can be repeated by the model: a prompt injection can ask it to print the token, and prompts are often stored in traces and logs. A copied token works outside the agent, so none of the agent’s controls apply. Keep secrets in a vault, attach them in code at call time, and return only results to the model.

mistakes.mistake: Using one shared API key for every user
mistakes.fix: Issue per-user delegated tokens so a leak or an injection reaches one account, and calls are attributable

mistakes.mistake: Requesting every scope at sign-up with long-lived tokens
mistakes.fix: Ask for read scopes first, add writes by step-up consent, and use short access tokens with silent refresh

quiz.question: A wealth app’s assistant calls its portfolio API with one shared service key for all 50,000 users. What is the main risk?
options: Higher token costs
A leak or a prompt injection can reach every user’s account, and calls cannot be tied to a user
Slower responses
The model cannot call tools in parallel
quiz.explanation: A shared key acts for everyone. Per-user delegated tokens limit any misuse to the user who consented and make calls attributable.

quiz.question: Why does the MCP authorization spec require PKCE in the authorization code flow?
options: It encrypts the access token
A stolen authorization code cannot be swapped for a token without the verifier only the client holds
It removes the need for scopes
It makes tokens last longer
quiz.explanation: PKCE binds the code to a secret verifier; an attacker who intercepts the redirect cannot redeem the code.

quiz.question: A claims assistant’s access token is placed in the system prompt so the model can "add the header". What is wrong?
options: Nothing, if the prompt is long enough
The model can be made to echo the token, and prompts end up in traces; the tool layer should attach it in code
Tokens in prompts expire faster
The API will reject tokens that pass through a model
quiz.explanation: Anything in the context can be repeated. Keep tokens in a vault and attach them at call time.

quiz.question: A wallet assistant only needs to read transaction history today. Which scope request is best at sign-up?
options: transactions:read only, with payout:write requested later if needed
Every scope the API offers, to avoid asking again
admin
No scope: the API will decide
quiz.explanation: Ask for read scopes first; add writes by step-up consent when the agent first needs them.

quiz.question: An attacker copies a 15-minute access token 5 minutes after it was issued. The refresh token stayed in the vault. For how many minutes can the attacker use the copied token?
options: Until the refresh token expires
quiz.explanation: 15 − 5 = 10 minutes. Without the refresh token the attacker cannot renew it.

quiz.question: A shared API key covering 50,000 accounts is rotated every 90 days. If it leaks just after rotation, how many account-hours are exposed?
A telecom assistant uses 1-hour access tokens with rotating refresh tokens. How often does a customer have to sign in again because of the short lifetime?
options: Every hour
Every day
Not because of the lifetime: refresh renews access silently
Only when they change phones
quiz.explanation: Short access tokens are renewed in the background; users only sign in again when the refresh token expires or is revoked.

quiz.question: 20,000 sellers use an assistant with 15-minute tokens; each seller’s tokens refresh 6 times a day. How many refresh calls hit the authorization server daily?
quiz.explanation: 20,000 × 6 = 120,000 refresh calls a day, a load the authorization server must be sized for.

quiz.question: Which choices shrink what a prompt injection in a fund factsheet can do through the agent’s tools? Select all that apply.
options: Per-user delegated tokens instead of a shared key
One scope per tool, so a read call carries no redeem rights
Keeping tokens in a vault the model never sees
A longer system prompt asking the model to ignore injections
quiz.explanation: Credentials limit reach and rights, and a vault keeps the secret out of reach; prompt wording alone is not a control.

quiz.question: A clinic’s assistant books appointments through a hospital API. An auditor asks which patient approved each booking. What makes this answerable?
options: One service key and a note in the prompt
Per-user delegated tokens and a log of user, tool and scope for every call
Longer token lifetimes
Storing the model’s reasoning
quiz.explanation: When each call carries the patient’s own consented token and is logged, every booking is attributable.

quiz.question: An MCP client gets a token for the bank’s statements server and forwards the same token to a third-party analytics API. What does the MCP spec say?
options: That is fine if the scopes match
Token passthrough is forbidden; tokens must be issued for the server that receives them
Only allowed over HTTPS
Allowed for read scopes
quiz.explanation: Tokens are bound to one audience with the resource parameter; passing them on breaks that boundary.

quiz.question: A user disconnects a lending assistant from their account. What should happen?
options: Keep the tokens in case they reconnect
Revoke the refresh token at the authorization server and delete the tokens from the vault
Shorten the next token’s lifetime
Log the user out of the website only
quiz.explanation: Revocation ends access; after the current short-lived access token expires, the agent can do nothing for that user.

quiz.question: Which are part of the MCP authorization approach for remote HTTP servers? Select all that apply.
options: OAuth 2.1 with PKCE
A resource indicator naming the MCP server the token is for
Protected resource metadata that points to the authorization server
Embedding the client secret in the tool description
quiz.explanation: MCP authorization builds on OAuth 2.1, PKCE, resource indicators and protected resource metadata; secrets never go in tool descriptions.

quiz.question: A policy assistant requests read and write scopes at sign-up, but 95% of sessions only read. What is the better design?
options: Keep broad scopes to avoid friction
Grant read scopes at sign-up and ask for write by step-up consent the first time it is needed
Remove write tools entirely
Use a shared key for writes
quiz.explanation: Incremental consent keeps most sessions read-only while writes remain possible with the user’s clear approval.

quiz.question: Users see a consent prompt about once every 30 days (refresh-token expiry) plus a step-up prompt on 0.2 writes a day. About how many prompts does a user see in 30 days?
Which of these belong in a tool-call audit record when agents act for users? Select all that apply.
options: The user the call acted for
The tool and the scope used
The time and the result status
The raw access token
quiz.explanation: Log who, what and when; never log the token itself, since logs are read by many people and systems.

quiz.question: A marketplace wants its assistant to use a refund API that only offers one all-powerful merchant key. What is the safest interim step?
options: Put the key in the prompt so the model can use it carefully
Keep the key in a vault behind a gateway that exposes narrow per-tool operations, checks the user and logs every call
Share the key with every seller
Give the model a copy for each session
quiz.explanation: When the API cannot scope tokens, the gateway must enforce the narrow operations and attribute each call itself.

quiz.question: Which grant type suits an agent acting for one signed-in customer against a bank API?
options: Client credentials: the app’s own identity
Authorization code with PKCE: the customer signs in and consents
Resource owner password: the agent stores the customer’s password
No grant: send the customer ID in a header
quiz.explanation: Client credentials act as the app, not the user; the password grant is removed in OAuth 2.1. Authorization code with PKCE yields a delegated token.

quiz.question: Refresh tokens are rotated: each use returns a new one and invalidates the old. A stolen old refresh token is presented. What should the authorization server do?
options: Issue a new access token
Reject it and, since reuse suggests theft, revoke the token family so the user signs in again
Extend its lifetime
Ignore it and log nothing
quiz.explanation: Reuse of a rotated refresh token signals theft; revoking the family cuts off both the attacker and the stale session.

quiz.question: Dhan Disha, a fictional wealth app, moves from a shared key in the prompt to per-user, per-tool, 15-minute tokens in a vault. Which results should it expect? Select all that apply.
options: A leaked credential exposes one account, read-only, for at most 15 minutes
Every tool call is attributable to a user
Users sign in every 15 minutes
An injection can no longer copy the credential out of the prompt
quiz.explanation: Refresh is silent, so short tokens do not add sign-ins; the other three follow from the new design.
